I'm Vishal, and I'm ten. This happened last month in games period.

We were playing kho-kho, and two captains picked teams. They picked and picked, and I was the last one standing by the wall. My face went hot. When I sat down, I told my sister Usha, who's in the same class, "Nobody ever picks me. I never win anything. Never."

Usha looked at me like I was crazy. "Bhai, you were captain in July. You picked me first."

"That was different."

"And your team won the relay on Sports Day."

I didn't want to hear it. It felt like one time was the real truth and all the other times didn't count.

The next week I got picked third. I didn't say anything to Usha. But I stopped saying "never" so much.

qa.q: When had Vishal been captain?
qa.a: He was captain in July.

qa.q: Why did being picked last once feel like "nobody ever picks me" to Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal felt embarrassed, and the hot feeling made that one moment seem like the whole truth. The good times, like being captain, felt as if they didn't count.

qa.q: What could Vishal try the next time he hears himself say "never"?
qa.a: He could stop and remember one time it wasn't true, like the relay on Sports Day. Checking for one counter-example stops one bad day from becoming a rule.

qa.q: How might Usha feel hearing Vishal say nobody ever picks him?
qa.a: Usha might feel confused or even a bit hurt, since Vishal picked Usha first in July. Usha seems to want to remind him of what really happened.

grounding: A boy picked last in one game says nobody ever picks him and he never wins, stretching a single event into a rule for life.

Class 3 teacher's note, Tuesday

In relay practice today the children chose their own teams. Tejas was chosen last. He stood at the line with his back to the others.

After the race, which his team lost, he sat under the gulmohar tree. "Nobody ever chooses me. I never win. I'll never win anything in my whole life." He said it three times.

I sat next to him. I didn't argue. I asked, "Who chose you for the quiz team last Friday?" He thought. "Hrithik." "And what happened?" "We won." He shrugged. "That was a quiz."

Hrithik came over and asked if Tejas wanted to try the baton pass again. Tejas said no, then went anyway.

Next step: tomorrow I'll make teams with numbered cards so choosing isn't public, and tell his mother what he said.

I'm Maria, and I share a room with Dilnaz in the women's hostel. Every exam season she says the same line: "I always freeze. I'll sit there and my brain will go white."

Last month, two weeks before semesters, she was saying it again when I handed her a pen. "Always? List the times you didn't."

She rolled her eyes, but she wrote. Statistics mid-term: fine. Economics viva: fine, even funny. Second-year finals: froze in one paper. I watched her add a column, "What was different?" Next to the good ones: "slept properly", "reached early", "started with a question I knew". Next to the frozen one: "stayed up all night, read notes in the corridor".

She sat back and stared at the page. "So I don't always freeze. I freeze when I don't sleep."

I can't say what she felt exactly. But the night before her first paper, she was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz write next to the frozen paper?
qa.a: "stayed up all night, read notes in the corridor".

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's line "So I don't always freeze. I freeze when I don't sleep" suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: She seems to have moved from a fixed rule about herself to a specific cause she can control. The counter-examples loosened the "always" and showed her what to work on.

qa.q: Why did adding the "What was different?" column help so much?
qa.a: It turned the list into clues: sleep, arriving early and starting with a known question went with the good exams. That gave Dilnaz concrete things to repeat.

qa.q: Why can Maria only guess at what Dilnaz felt?
qa.a: Maria sees the list, the stare at the page and the early night, but not what's inside. Maria reads the early sleep as a sign the lesson landed.

grounding: A roommate watches a student who believes she always freezes in exams list times she didn't and what was different, loosening the rule.

Monday: In the engineering college canteen, Karthik pushed away his dosa. "Thermodynamics on Saturday. I always freeze in exams, Sabina. Every single time."

Sabina stirred her tea. "Every single time? Name them."

Wednesday: Karthik sat in the library with a notebook, a bit annoyed that he'd agreed to do this. Exams in two years: fourteen. Froze: three. He looked at the three. All were first papers of the semester, all after cramming till 3 a.m. The eleven good ones: he'd done a timed practice paper the week before.

"Three out of fourteen," he told Sabina, sounding almost disappointed. "That's not always."

Saturday: The night before, he did a timed practice paper and slept at eleven. In the hall his hands shook when he saw question one. He skipped to question three, which he knew. By the time he came back, his head had cleared.

He didn't feel brave. He felt prepared.

qa.q: How many exams did Karthik freeze in?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Karthik sound "almost disappointed" when he said "That's not always"?
qa.a: The "always" rule had become part of how Karthik saw himself, so losing it felt strange, even though it was good news. It also meant he now had to act on what he learned.

qa.q: What did Karthik learn from the three freezes, and how did he use it?
qa.a: They were all first papers after cramming till 3 a.m., while good ones followed a timed practice paper. So he did a practice paper, slept at eleven, and skipped to a question he knew when he shook.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel if she heard Karthik say he felt prepared, not brave?
qa.a: Sabina would probably be pleased and a little proud that her simple question led somewhere. She might see that he now trusts evidence more than the old rule.

grounding: Over a week a student who believes he always freezes in exams counts the times he didn't, finds what was different, and uses it.

Now he was back in his parents' flat in Pune, and it had rained for nine days.

His sister Nikita put her phone in front of him. "A small café in Aundh. They want a cook. The owner's a woman who used to be a teacher. Reviews say she's lovely to staff."

"Every kitchen is the same," Gautam said. "They all scream. They all use you. I'm not doing that again."

"You worked in one kitchen."

"One was enough to know."

Nikita left the phone on the table. He didn't touch it. That evening he searched for data-entry jobs he didn't want, because at least they weren't kitchens. The rain kept falling.

The quarterly review at the city museum's education department had gone well, Dilnaz thought. Maria's school tours were the most booked in the building.

So she was surprised, an hour later, to find Maria in the storeroom, sorting worksheets that didn't need sorting, jaw tight.

"All okay?"

"You said I need to delegate more," Maria said. "In front of everyone. So I'm basically not good enough to lead."

Dilnaz went back to her desk, printed the review, and came back. "Can I read you the whole page?"

She read it aloud, slowly. "Tours booked out every week. Teachers ask for you by name. Your new worksheet for Class 5 is now used across the department. You trained two volunteers. One area to grow: delegate more so you don't burn out."

She handed the page over. "What else does it say?"

Maria read it again, silently. Her shoulders came down a little. "It says I'm doing well," she said. "And one thing to work on."

Today in art, Sir held up my drawing of the mango tree behind our school and said to the class, "Look at the light through the leaves. Mridul, how did you do this?"
